14: \begin{document}

16: \preprint{FERMILAB-Pub-02/165-T}

18: \title{Fully differential $W^\prime$ production and decay at next-to-leading
19: order in QCD}
20: 
21: \author{Zack Sullivan}
22: \address{Theoretical Physics Department, Fermi National
23: Accelerator Laboratory, Batavia, IL, 60510-0500}
24: 
25: \date{July 23, 2002}
26: 
27: \maketitle
28: 
29: \begin{abstract}
30: We present the fully differential production and decay of a $W^\prime$
31: boson, with arbitrary vector and axial-vector couplings, to any final
32: state at next-to-leading order in QCD.  We demonstrate a complete
33: factorization of couplings at next-to-leading order in both the
34: partial width of the $W^\prime$ boson, and in the full two-to-two
35: cross section.  We provide numerical predictions for the contribution
36: of a $W^\prime$ boson to single-top-quark production, and separate
37: results based on whether the mass of the right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$
38: is light enough for the leptonic decay channel to be open.  The
39: single-top-quark analysis will allow for an improved direct $W^\prime$
40: mass limit of 525--550~GeV using data from run I of the Fermilab
41: Tevatron.  We propose a modified tolerance method for estimating
42: parton distribution function uncertainties in cross sections.
43: \end{abstract}
44: 
45: \section{Introduction}
46: 
47: Since the introduction of the standard model, many extensions have
48: been proposed that involve enhanced gauge symmetries.  One common
49: feature of these models is the prediction of additional gauge bosons,
50: generically called \wpr and $Z^\prime$ bosons.  In non-universal and
51: top-flavor models, the \wpr gauge boson arises from a new SU(2)$_L$
52: sector that distinguishes between generations of fermions
53: \cite{Li:nk,Malkawi:1996fs,Muller:1996dj}, and may treat quarks and
54: leptons differently \cite{Georgi:1989ic,Georgi:1989xz,He:1999vp}.  The
55: \wpr boson could be the lowest Kaluza-Klein mode of the $W$ boson
56: \cite{Datta:2000gm}, or a heavy mass eigenstate in non-commuting
57: extended technicolor \cite{Chivukula:1995gu}.  In a left-right
58: symmetric model the \wpr and standard-model $W$ bosons are remnants of
59: a broken ${\mathrm SU(2)}_L \times {\mathrm SU(2)}_R$ symmetry
60: \cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974hk,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk}.
61: The resulting left-right mixing may be naturally suppressed by
62: orbifold breaking of the left-right symmetry \cite{Mimura:2002te}, or
63: by supersymmetric interactions \cite{Cvetic:1983su}.  While indirect
64: bounds may be placed on the masses and couplings of these various \wpr
65: bosons within the context of their explicit theories, it is always
66: advantageous to search for these new particles directly.  In order to
67: facilitate a direct experimental search, and to achieve the most
68: general contact with theory, we calculate the fully differential
69: next-to-leading order cross section for the production and decay of a
70: \wpr boson to any final state with arbitrary vector and axial-vector
71: couplings.
72: 
73: The most general Lorentz invariant Lagrangian describing the coupling
74: of a \wpr to fermions may be written as
75: \beq
76: {\cal L} = \frac{g}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{f}_i\gamma_\mu \bigl(
77: C^R_{f_if_j} P_R + C^L_{f_if_j} P_L \bigr) W^{\prime} f_j +
78: \mathrm{H.c.} \,, \label{eq:genlan}
79: \eeq
80: where $P_{R,L}=(1\pm \gamma_5)/2$, $g$ is the standard model SU(2)$_L$
81: coupling, and the $C^{R,L}_{f_if_j}$ are arbitrary couplings that
82: differ for quarks and leptons.  For a standard model $W$ boson,
83: $C^R=0$, and $C^L$ is either the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix or
84: diagonal, for quarks or leptons, respectively.
85: 
86: Most experimental searches have concentrated on \wpr bosons that decay
87: via a purely left- or right-handed current.  In order to make contact
88: with these results, we rewrite Eq.~(\ref{eq:genlan}) in the notation
89: typical of left-right symmetric models as \cite{Langacker:1989xa}
90: \beq
91: {\cal L} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{f}_i\gamma_\mu \bigl( g_R
92: e^{i\omega} \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} P_R + g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j}
93: P_L\bigr) W^{\prime} f_j + \mathrm{H.c.} \,, \label{eq:lagrangian}
94: \eeq
95: where $\zeta$ is a left-right mixing angle, and $\omega$ is a
96: CP-violating phase that can be absorbed into $V^R$.  In this notation,
97: $g_{R(L)}$ are the right (left) gauge couplings, and
98: $V^{R,L}_{f_if_j}$ are generalized Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (GCKM)
99: matrices.  In models where the $W$ and \wpr mix, the mixing angle
100: $\zeta$ is usually constrained to be small ($|\zeta|<$ a few $\times
101: 10^{-5}$--$10^{-2}$ \cite{Groom:in}).  Hence, the search for purely
102: right- or left-handed states appears well motivated.
103: 
104: Many direct searches for \wpr bosons have been performed at hadron
105: colliders.  Most experimental analyses have considered left- or
106: right-handed \wpr bosons, with standard-model-like couplings, that
107: decay into leptonic final states.  Left-handed $W^\prime_L$ bosons, or
108: right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons in which the decay into a
109: right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ is kinematically allowed, are
110: constrained to have masses $m_{\wprm} > 786$~GeV
111: \cite{Arnison:1983zy,Arnison:ut,Ansari:1987ch,Albajar:1988ka,Abe:1994zg,Abachi:1995yi,Abe:1999gz,Affolder:2001gr}.
112: If $m_{\nu_R} \agt m_{\wprm}$ the decay to $\nu_R$ is not allowed,
113: and the right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons are only directly constrained
114: by peak searches in the dijet data.  Unless the \wpr has greatly
115: enhanced couplings to light quarks, the dijet data are limited by QCD
116: backgrounds to providing a mass limit of $420$~GeV
117: \cite{Alitti:1990kw,Alitti:1993pn,Abe:1997hm}.
118: 
119: The only final state not measured by one of the experiments listed
120: above involves the decay of a \wpr to a single top quark.  In
121: Refs.~\cite{Simmons:1996ws,Tait:1997fe} it was pointed out that a
122: deviation of measured the single-top-quark cross section from the
123: standard model prediction could be evidence of a new gauge
124: interaction.  In the context of models with \wpr bosons, we wish to
125: take this one step further, and propose that the experiments search
126: for an explicit \wpr mass peak in the $s$-channel single-top-quark
127: sample.  We examine just how large the cross section into single top
128: quarks can be at the Fermilab Tevatron and Large Hadron Collider (LHC)
129: as a function of \wpr mass, and determine how enhanced or suppressed
130: couplings enter into the measurable cross section after cuts.  We also
131: determine the next-to-leading order distributions of the final-state
132: jets to estimate the effect on the reconstruction of the \wpr mass
133: peak.
134: 
135: A \wpr boson that propagates in the $s$-channel appears very similar
136: to Drell-Yan production.  We might be tempted to use the
137: next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) predictions for Drell-Yan
138: \cite{Hamberg:1990np} (or the updates in
139: Ref.~\cite{Harlander:2002wh}).  However, these calculations are not
140: adequate to predict the cross section for \wpr bosons which decay to
141: quarks.  There are two reasons for this.  The first problem is that
142: the final state effects are very large.  Not only are there large QCD
143: corrections to the quark final state, but the top-quark mass has a
144: large effect on the branching fraction when it is in the final state.
145: The second reason is that there are initial- and final-state
146: interference terms that arise at NNLO that are of an unknown size.
147: (Pure QCD processes also interfere at NNLO, e.g.\ with $u\bar d \to
148: u\bar d$ via the exchange of two gluons.)  Therefore, we cannot simply
149: take the NNLO production as calculated and append a Breit-Wigner
150: propagator that uses leading or next-to-leading order widths.
151: Instead, we perform the complete calculation at next-to-leading order.
152: 
153: We organize the paper as follows.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:width} we
154: calculate the partial widths into leptons or quarks, including the
155: effects of the top-quark mass, for the \wpr boson using arbitrary
156: vector and axial-vector couplings at next-to-leading order (NLO) in
157: QCD.  We demonstrate that the couplings factorize, and present some
158: numerical results for partial widths and branching fractions into a
159: top-quark final state.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma} we calculate the fully
160: differential production and decay of a \wpr into any final state at
161: NLO in QCD.  We present numerical results for the single-top-quark
162: production cross section via $s$-channel exchange of a \wpr boson.  We
163: asses all theoretical uncertainties, and propose a modification of the
164: tolerance method for calculating parton distribution function
165: uncertainties.  Finally, we present the NLO jet distributions, discuss
166: the effect of jet definitions on these distributions, and estimate the
167: limits that may be placed on the \wpr mass using data from run I and
168: run II of the Fermilab Tevatron.
169: 
170: \section{Next-to-leading order width}
171: \label{sec:width}
172: 
173: We divide our evaluation of the \wpr width into three terms that
174: depend on the final decay products:
175: \beq
176: \Gamma_{\mathrm tot}(\wprm) = \Gamma (\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)
177: +\Gamma (\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime) + \Gamma (\wprm\to l\bar\nu) \,.
178: \label{eq:widfact}
179: \eeq
180: We separate the partial widths containing a top quark from those
181: containing only massless quarks so that we may retain an explicit
182: top-quark mass dependence in the width.
183: 
184: While the large number of couplings in Eq.~(\ref{eq:lagrangian})
185: appears daunting, a factorization of the couplings occurs in the
186: partial widths of Eq.~(\ref{eq:widfact}) that greatly simplifies the
187: calculation.  The leading order partial widths are
188: \bea
189: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)&=&
190: \frac{g^2\beta^2}{16\pi m_{\wprm}} |V^\prime_{tq^\prime}|^2 (m^2_{\wprm}
191: + m^2_t/2)\,, \label{eq:wlot} \\
192: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
193: |V^\prime_{qq^\prime}|^2 m_{\wprm} \,, \label{eq:wloq} \\
194: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to l\bar\nu)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
195: |V^\prime_{l\nu}|^2 \frac{m_{\wprm}}{3} \,, \label{eq:wlol}
196: \eea
197: where $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, and we assume $g^2=8 m^2_W
198: G_F/\sqrt{2}$, as in the standard model.  Because we have assumed there
199: is at most one non-zero mass in the final state, the couplings appear
200: only in the combination
201: \beq
202: \bigl| g V^\prime_{f_if_j}\bigr|^2 \equiv 
203: \bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 + \bigl| g_R
204: \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 \,. \label{eq:vprime}
205: \eeq
206: Hence, the partial widths of the \wpr boson have the same form as the
207: standard model $W$ boson, with the effect of new couplings and GCKM
208: matrix elements absorbed into $V^\prime_{f_if_j}$.
209: 
210: The above factorization of couplings turns out to hold in the
211: next-to-leading order widths as well.  The calculations of the
212: next-to-leading order partial widths of the $W$ boson were first
213: performed for the massless \cite{Albert:ix}, one mass
214: \cite{Alvarez:1987gi}, and arbitrary mass \cite{Lahanas:1996xx} final
215: states many years ago.  In order to derive the factorization of
216: arbitrary couplings above, however, we rederive the partial widths,
217: but use a newer calculational method whose results are needed in the
218: calculation of the fully differential cross section in
219: Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma}.
220: 
221: We evaluate the next-to-leading order partial widths to quarks by
222: using the phase-space-slicing method with two cutoffs
223: \cite{Harris:2001sx}.  In this method, phase space is divided into
224: three regions: soft (S), hard collinear (HC), and hard non-collinear
225: (H$\overline{\mathrm C}$).  The first two regions are integrated over
226: two-body phase space in $n=4-2\epsilon$ dimensions, whereas the third
227: region is integrated over three-body phase space in 4 dimensions with
228: cuts.
229: 
230: The soft region of phase space is defined in the \wpr rest frame by
231: a condition on the energy of the emitted gluon
232: \begin{equation}
233: \label{eq:appsg}
234:   E_g \leq \delta_s\, \frac{m_{\wprm}}{2} \,,
235: \end{equation}
236: where $\delta_s$ is an arbitrary parameter that must cancel in the
237: final result.  The hard region is the complement, $E_g > \delta_s\,
238: m_{\wprm}/2$. The gluon can only be collinear with a light quark, and
239: so the collinear region is defined by comparing the invariant mass
240: squared of the gluon and light quark to $\delta_c m^2_{\wprm}$, i.e.\
241: the collinear region is $s_{qg} = 2p_q\cdot p_g < \delta_c
242: m^2_{\wprm}$, where $p_{q,g}$ are quark and gluon four-momenta.  The
243: final result must be independent of $\delta_c$.  In practice we retain
244: terms logarithmic in $\delta_s$ or $\delta_c$, and drop terms that are
245: linear in the cutoffs.  At the end, we take the couplings numerically
246: to zero and show the solution contains no residual $\delta_s$ or
247: $\delta_c$ dependence.
248: 
249: The two-body next-to-leading order correction to the width is given by
250: \beq
251: \delta\Gamma_{2} = \frac{\alpha_s (m_{W^\prime})}{2\pi} C_F ( M^2_S + M^2_C
252: + M^2_V + \widetilde{M}^2_V ) \Gamma_{\mathrm LO} \,, \label{eq:wid2}
253: \eeq
254: where $C_F = 4/3$, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}$ is listed in
255: Eqs.~(\ref{eq:wlot}, \ref{eq:wloq}).  If there is a top quark in the final
256: state, the terms are
257: \bea
258: M^2_S &=&2\ln^2(\delta_s) - 2\ln (\delta_s) \left[ 1 - \ln \left(
259: \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \right] + \frac{\mwpsq + \mtsq}{\mwpsq -
260: \mtsq} \ln\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) - 2 {\mathrm Li}_2(\beta)
261: - \frac{1}{2}\ln^2\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \,,
262: \label{eq:msf} \\
263: M^2_C &=& \frac{7}{2} - 2\zeta_2 - \ln^2(\delta_s) + 2 {\mathrm Li}_2\!
264: \left( \frac{\beta \delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - \ln^2 (\beta) +2 \ln
265: (\delta_s) \ln (\beta) - \ln (\delta_c) \left( 2 \ln (\delta_s) +
266: \frac{3}{2} - 2 \ln (\beta) \right) \,, \label{eq:mcf} \\
267: M^2_V &=& -\frac{1}{2}\ln^2\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) -
268: \frac{5}{2}\ln\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) - \ln (1 - \lambda)
269: \left[ 2 + \beta + 2 \ln\! \left(
270: \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \right] \nonumber \\
271: && - 6 - \ln^2 (1 - \lambda) + 2 {\mathrm Li}_2(\lambda) - 2\zeta_2 \,, 
272: \label{eq:mvf} \\
273: \widetilde{M}^2_V &=& \frac{\beta (1-\beta)}{2 (3-\beta)}\ln(1 - \lambda) \,,
274: \eea
275: where $\zeta_2 = \pi^2/6$, $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, and $\lambda =
276: 1/\beta$.  Note $(1 -\lambda) < 0$, which means $\ln (1 -\lambda) = \ln
277: |1 -\lambda|$, but $\ln^2 (1 -\lambda) = \ln^2 |1 -\lambda| - \pi^2$.
278: 
279: If both final-state quarks are massless, the formulae simplify to
280: \bea
281: M^2_S &=&4\ln^2(\delta_s) \,, \\
282: M^2_C &=& 7 - 4\zeta_2 - 2 \ln^2(\delta_s) + 4 {\mathrm Li}_2\! \left(
283: \frac{\delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - \ln (\delta_c) [ 4 \ln (\delta_s)
284: + 3 ] \,, \\
285: M^2_V &=& - 8 + 4 \zeta_2 \,, \\
286: \widetilde{M}^2_V &=& 0 \,.
287: \eea
288: The sum of the terms in the massless case is
289: \beq
290: M^2 = 2\ln^2(\delta_s) - \ln
291: (\delta_c) [ 4 \ln (\delta_s) + 3 ] + 4 {\mathrm Li}_2\! \left(
292: \frac{\delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - 1 \,. \label{eq:mmsq}
293: \eeq
294: 
295: \newcommand{\sttp}{s^\prime_{23}}
296: \newcommand{\sot}{s^{}_{13}}
297: \newcommand{\sotp}{s^\prime_{12}}
298: 
299: The three-body hard non-collinear real gluon emission term is evaluated
300: using a Monte Carlo integration in four dimensions, subject to the
301: cuts listed above.  The integrand is given by
302: \beq
303: d(\delta\Gamma_{3}) = \frac{1}{64\pi^3 m_{W^\prime}}
304: \overline{\Sigma}|M_3|^2 dE_g dE_{q^{\prime}} \; ,
305: \eeq
306: with
307: \beq
308: \overline{\Sigma}|M_3|^2 = -2\pi\alpha_s g^2 C_F
309: |V^{\prime}_{tq^\prime}|^2 \Psi_\Gamma \;,
310: \eeq
311: and
312: \bea
313: \Psi_\Gamma&=& 
314: 2\beta m_{\wprm}^2 (3-\beta)\biggl( \frac{\sotp}{\sot \sttp}
315: -\frac{m^2_t}{s^{\prime\,2}_{23}} \biggr) \nonumber \\
316: &&+ (3-\beta) \biggl(
317: \frac{\sot}{\sttp} + \frac{\sttp}{\sot} \biggr)
318: +2 (1-\beta) \;, \label{eq:appwid}
319: \eea
320: where $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, $\sotp = 2p_1\cdot p_2$, $\sot =
321: 2p_1\cdot p_3$, $\sttp = 2p_2\cdot p_3$, and $p_1$, $p_2$, and $p_3$
322: are the four-momenta of the light quark, top quark, and gluon,
323: respectively.  When both quarks are massless $\beta = 1$, and
324: Eq.~(\ref{eq:appwid}) is very simple.
325: 
326: Once we determine that the factorization of couplings holds for all
327: terms, the partial widths reduce to the expressions given in
328: Ref.~\cite{Alvarez:1987gi} with the replacement of CKM matrix elements
329: by the GCKM matrix elements $|V^\prime|^2$ defined in
330: Eq.~(\ref{eq:vprime}).  The massless case is simply
331: \beq
332: \Gamma_{\mathrm NLO}(\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime) = \biggl( 1 +
333: \frac{\alpha_s(m_{\wprm})}{\pi} \biggr) \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to
334: q{\bar q}^\prime) \,.
335: \eeq
336: The massive case should reduce to Eq.~(12) of Ref.~\cite{Alvarez:1987gi},
337: \bea
338: \Gamma_{\mathrm NLO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime) &=&
339: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime) + \frac{g^2}{16\pi}
340: \frac{\alpha_s(m_{\wprm})}{4\pi} C_F |V^\prime_{tq^\prime}|^2 m_{\wprm}
341: \nonumber \\
342: &&\hspace*{8em} \times\{ \beta(1-\beta)(\beta-4) -
343: \beta^2(9-5\beta)\ln(\beta) - (1-\beta)
344: (4+6\beta-5\beta^2)\ln(1-\beta) 
345: \nonumber \\
346: &&\hspace*{9em} + \beta^2(3-\beta) [3/2 + 4 {\mathrm
347: Li }_2 (1-\beta) + 2 \ln(\beta)\ln(1-\beta) ] \} \,. \label{eq:alvwid}
348: \eea
349: 
350: 
351: \subsection{Numerical results}
352: \label{sec:numwid}
353: 
354: In order to be of immediate use to experimental analyses at the
355: Fermilab Tevatron, we make definite predictions of the \wpr partial
356: and total widths.  In all numerical results we use $m_t=175\pm 5$ GeV,
357: $G_F=1.16639\times 10^{-5}$ GeV$^{-2}$, and $m_W=80.4$ GeV.  We use a
358: two-loop running of $\alpha_s$ as defined in the CTEQ5M1 parton
359: distribution functions \cite{Lai:1999wy}.  We assume that
360: $V^\prime_{l\nu}$ is the identity matrix, and for
361: $V^\prime_{qq^\prime}$ we use the average Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa
362: (CKM) matrix \cite{Groom:in} with the exception that we assume
363: $|V^\prime_{tb}|=1$,
364: \beq
365: V^\prime_{\mathrm CKM} = \left(
366: \begin{array}{llc}
367: 0.9751 & 0.2215 & 0.0035 \\
368: 0.2210 & 0.9743 & 0.0410 \\
369: 0.0090 & 0.0400 & 1.0000
370: \end{array}
371: \right) \,. \label{eq:ckm}
372: \eeq
373: 
374: \begin{figure}[tbh]
375: \epsfxsize=3.375in
376: \centerline{\epsfbox{cwpss.ps}} 
377: \caption{Dependence of the NLO correction to the \wpr width on
378: $\delta_s = 300\times \delta_c$, for $m_{W^{\prime}}=500$ GeV.
379: $\delta\Gamma_{\mathrm NLO} = \delta\Gamma_2 + \delta\Gamma_3$, where

387: Before we discuss our results, we must show that our final result does
388: not depend on the cutoffs we choose.  To demonstrate this, we fix the
389: ratio of $\delta_s/\delta_c = 300$, and plot in Fig.~\ref{fig:wpss}
390: the NLO correction to the width of a \wpr of mass 500~GeV.  In the
391: upper half of the figure we see the logarithmic dependence in
392: $\delta_s$ and $\delta_c$ of the two- and three-body terms,
393: $\delta\Gamma_2$ and $\delta\Gamma_3$.  In the bottom half of the
394: figure we focus on the sum of the correction terms
395: $\delta\Gamma_{\mathrm NLO}$ for various values of $\delta_s$
396: (circles), and compare the result to the analytic prediction (solid
397: line) of Eq.~(\ref{eq:alvwid}).  Once $\delta_s \alt 10^{-3}$
398: ($\delta_c \alt 1/3\times 10^{-5}$), the result is stable to much less
399: than $1\%$ of the known NLO correction.
400: In practice there is a tradeoff between numerical accuracy in
401: canceling the logarithmic divergences of $\delta_s$ and $\delta_c$ in
402: the Monte Carlo, and the residual power suppressed dependence on these
403: parameters.  Hence, we always choose values of $\delta_s$ and
404: $\delta_c$ to ensure that the residual effects are smaller than the
405: desired Monte Carlo statistical error.

535: It is not surprising that top-quark threshold effects cause a large
536: uncertainty in the branching fraction for \wpr masses less than 300
537: GeV.  This also appears in the large increase in branching fraction at
538: NLO over the LO branching fraction.  With 33\% changes in both the
539: mass variation and NLO correction, perturbation theory is somewhat
540: suspect if $m_{\wprm} \sim 200$ GeV.  However, the effect is less than
541: 10\% by 225 GeV, and rapidly vanishes as $m^2_{\wprm} \gg m^2_t$.  The
542: branching fraction into a top-quark final state is nearly saturated at
543: $1/3$ ($1/4$) when $m_{\wprm} \sim 500$~GeV for the quark-only
544: (quark-plus-lepton) model of decays.  Hence, a large fraction of \wpr
545: events should produce a top-quark in the final state.  In
546: Sec.~\ref{sec:tottop} we see this effect on the single-top-quark cross
547: section.

550: 
551: \section{Next-to-leading order cross section}
552: \label{sec:sigma}
553: 
554: The analytic form of the differential production and decay of a \wpr
555: at next-to-leading order is very similar to that of $s$-channel
556: single-top-quark production.  The complete calculation of differential
557: single-top-quark production using the phase space slicing method
558: appears in Ref.~\cite{Harris:2002md}.  We generalize the calculation
559: in that paper to the production of one massive particle through a \wpr
560: boson (such that single-top-quark production is a special case).  We
561: follow closely the notation of Ref.~\cite{Harris:2002md}, but retain
562: arbitrary couplings in the vertices.  We note that the $t$-channel
563: exchange of a virtual \wpr is suppressed by at least
564: $1/m^4_{W^\prime}$, and hence do not consider it here.  However, the
565: analytic expressions and factorizations that follow are valid for this
566: channel as well.  The analytic formulae for the $t$-channel exchange
567: may be obtained by simple crossing.
568: 
569: At leading order, the production of a heavy quark (lepton) may be
570: written schematically as
571: \begin{equation}
572: u(p_1)\bar d(p_2) \to \wprmp \to \bar b(p_3) t(p_4) [\bar l(p_3)
573: \nu(p_4)] \,,
574: \end{equation}
575: where $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$, $u\bar d$ represents all possible parton
576: fluxes, and the heavy particle in the final state ($t$ or $\nu_R$) has
577: four-momentum $p_4$ and mass $m$.
578: 
579: The leading-order fully differential spin-averaged partonic cross
580: section can be written as
581: \begin{equation}
582: d\sigma_{0} = \frac{1}{2s} \overline{\sum}
583: \left|{\cal M}_{0}\right|^2 d {\mathrm{PS}}_2 \,,
584: \end{equation}
585: where $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is the partonic center-of-momentum energy
586: squared, and the two body phase space is given by
587: \begin{equation}
588: d{\mathrm{PS}}_2 = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2} \frac{d^3 p_3}{2 E_3} \frac{d^3
589:    p_4}{2 E_4} \delta^{(4)}(q-p_3-p_4)\, .
590: \end{equation}
591: 
592: The matrix element squared, summed (averaged) over final- (initial-)
593: state spin and color states, for production of one massive particle is
594: \begin{equation}
595: \overline{\sum} \left|{\cal M}_{0}\right|^2 = \frac{2N_c}{3} \frac{R_t
596: t\bigl( t-m^2\bigr) + R_u u\bigl( u-m^2\bigr)}{\bigl( s-\mwpsq
597: \bigr)^2 +\mwpsq \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2} \,,
598: \end{equation}
599: where $t=(p_1-p_3)^2$, $u=(p_2-p_3)^2$. The number of colors $N_c=3$,
600: and $m = m_t$, for a final state with a top quark.  For the production
601: of a massive neutrino $m = m_{\nu_R}$ and $N_c=1$.  If the final state
602: is massless, simply set $m=0$ and use $N_c=3$ (1) for quarks
603: (leptons).  The functions $R_t$ and $R_u$ are given by
604: \bea
605: R_t&=&\bigl( |V_i|^2+|A_i|^2 \bigr) \bigl( |V_f|^2+|A_f|^2 \bigr) +
606: 4 {\mathrm Re } (V_i{A_i}^{\!\ast}) {\mathrm Re } (V_f\!{A_f}^{\!\ast}) \,,
607: \label{eq:rt} \\
608: R_u&=&\bigl( |V_i|^2+|A_i|^2 \bigr) \bigl( |V_f|^2+|A_f|^2 \bigr) -
609: 4 {\mathrm Re } (V_i{A_i}^{\!\ast}) {\mathrm Re } (V_f\!{A_f}^{\!\ast}) \,,
610: 
611: \label{eq:ru}
612: \eea
613: where $V_{i,f}$ and $A_{i,f}$ are the vector and axial-vector
614: couplings for the initial- and final-state vertices, respectively.  In
615: the notation of Eq.~(\ref{eq:lagrangian}),
616: \bea
617: |V|^2+|A|^2 &=& \frac{\bigl| g_R \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2
618: +\bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2}{4} \,, \\
619: 2 {\mathrm Re } (V\! A^{\ast}) &=& \frac{\bigl| g_R \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j}
620: \bigr|^2 -\bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2}{4} \,.
621: \eea
622: For right- or left-handed \wpr bosons $|V|=|A|$, $R_u = 0$, $R_t$
623: reduces to $R_t = \bigl( g^4 |V^\prime_i|^2 |V^\prime_f|^2 \bigr) /8$,
624: and we recover the standard model $s$-channel single-top-quark cross
625: section published in Refs.~\cite{Harris:2002md,Harris:2000sv},
626: including the Breit-Wigner term, up to the GCKM couplings.
627: 
628: We calculate the fully differential next-to-leading order cross
629: section with the same method used in Sec.~\ref{sec:width}.
630: Again, the phase space is divided into a hard and soft region, where
631: the soft region is now defined in the partonic center-of-momentum
632: frame by a condition of the emitted gluon energy:
633: \begin{equation}
634:   E_g \leq \delta_s\, \frac{\sqrt{s_{12}}}{2} \,,
635: \end{equation}
636: where $s_{ij}=(p_i+p_j)^2$.  The hard region is the complement, $E_g >
637: \delta_s\, \sqrt{s_{12}}/2$.  A region is collinear if an invariant
638: in a propagator is less than $\delta_c s_{12}$, i.e.\ the region is
639: collinear if in a denominator we obtain $s_{ij} = (p_i+p_j)^2 <
640: \delta_c s_{12}$, or $t_{ij} = (p_i-p_j)^2 < \delta_c s_{12}$.
641: 
642: At next-to-leading order, color conservation forbids the exchange of a
643: single gluon between the initial and final states.  This is convenient
644: when organizing the solution, because the leptonic cross section only
645: has QCD corrections in the initial state.  Hence, we list separately
646: the initial and final state corrections.
647: 
648: The two-body NLO correction to the partonic cross section contains
649: \begin{equation}
650: d\sigma_2 = \frac{\alpha_s}{2\pi} C_F [(M_S^2 + M_C^2 + M_V^2)d\sigma_0
651: +d\tilde{\sigma}_V] \,, \label{eq:dsig2}
652: \end{equation}
653: where $C_F=4/3$, and $d\tilde{\sigma}_V$ is the part of the correction
654: to the vertex containing the top quark that is not proportional to the
655: LO cross section.  If the final state does not contain a top quark
656: then $d\tilde{\sigma}_V=0$; otherwise,
657: \begin{equation}
658: d\tilde{\sigma}_V = (R_t + R_u) \frac{t u}{s^2}\frac{m_t^2 \ln(1-
659: \lambda)}{\bigl( s-\mwpsq\bigr)^2 +\mwpsq \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2} 
660: d{\mathrm{PS}}_2 \,.
661: \end{equation}
662: 
663: The initial-state corrections appearing in Eq.~(\ref{eq:dsig2}) are
664: \bea
665: M^2_{S i} &=& 4\ln^2(\delta_s) \,, \\
666: M^2_{C i} &=& [4\ln(\delta_s) + 3] \ln\!\left( \frac{s}{\mu^2_F}\right)
667: \,, \\
668: M^2_{V i} &=& -8+4\zeta_2 \,,
669: \eea
670: where $\zeta_2 = \pi^2/6$, and $\mu_F$ is the factorization scale.
671: If there is a top quark in the final state, $M^2_{S f}$, $M^2_{C f}$,
672: and $M^2_{V f}$ are the same as those listed in
673: Eqs.~(\ref{eq:msf}--\ref{eq:mvf}), with the replacements $\mwpsq \to s$,
674: $\beta \to 1-m_t^2/s$, and $\lambda = 1/\beta$.  If both quarks in the
675: final state are massless, then $M^2_f$ is given by Eq.~(\ref{eq:mmsq}).
676: 
677: The complete two-body cross section is given by
678: \begin{equation}
679: \sigma_2 = \sum_{a,b} \int dx_1 dx_2 \{ f_a^{H_1}(x_1,\mu_F)
680: f_b^{H_2}(x_2,\mu_F) d\sigma_2^{a b} + [ \tilde{f}_a^{H_1}(x_1,\mu_F)
681: f_b^{H_2}(x_2,\mu_F) + f_a^{H_1}(x_1,\mu_F)
682: \tilde{f}_b^{H_2}(x_2,\mu_F) ] d\sigma_0^{a b} \} \,,
683: \end{equation}
684: where $a$, $b$ sum over all quark-antiquark luminosities, $\mu_F$ is
685: the factorization scale, $H_{1,2}$ are the initial-state hadrons, and
686: the $f(x,\mu)$ are NLO parton distribution functions.  The $\tilde{f}$
687: functions are introduced to compensate for a difference between the
688: limits of integration used in the phase space slicing calculation of
689: the initial-state collinear singularities and the modified minimal
690: subtraction $\overline{\mathrm MS}$ scheme used in the NLO parton
691: distribution functions.  The $\tilde{f}$ functions are given in
692: Ref.~\cite{Harris:2001sx}.
693: 
694: 
695: \renewcommand{\sot}{s^{}_{12}}
696: \newcommand{\stfp}{s^{\prime}_{34}}
697: \newcommand{\stf}{s^{}_{35}}
698: \newcommand{\sffp}{s^{\prime}_{45}}
699: \newcommand{\tot}{t^{}_{13}}
700: \newcommand{\ttt}{t^{}_{23}}
701: \newcommand{\tofp}{t^{\prime}_{14}}
702: \newcommand{\ttfp}{t^{\prime}_{24}}
703: \newcommand{\tof}{t^{}_{15}}
704: \newcommand{\ttf}{t^{}_{25}}
705: 
706: 
707: The three-body hard non-collinear terms are evaluated using a Monte
708: Carlo integration in four dimensions, subject to the cuts listed
709: above.  The cross section is given by
710: \begin{eqnarray}
711: \sigma_3 &=& - \sum_{a,b} \int dx_1 dx_2 \frac{4\pi\alpha_s}{s}
712: \int_{\mathrm H\overline{C}} \{ f^{H_1}_{q_a}(x_1,\mu_F)
713: f^{H_2}_{q_b}(x_2,\mu_F) \Psi_{q\bar q} \nonumber \\
714: &&\hspace*{12em} + [ f^{H_1}_{q_a}(x_1,\mu_F) f^{H_2}_{g}(x_2,\mu_F) +
715: f^{H_1}_{g}(x_1,\mu_F) f^{H_2}_{q_b}(x_2,\mu_F) ] \Psi_{qg} \}
716: d{\mathrm{PS}}_3 \,.
717: \end{eqnarray}
718: If we label the momenta in the three-body processes
719: \bea
720: \Psi_{q\bar q}: u(p_1) \bar d(p_2) &\to & \bar b(p_3) t(p_4) g(p_5) \,, \\
721: \Psi_{qg}: u(p_1) g(p_2) &\to & \bar b(p_3) t(p_4) d(p_5) \,,
722: \eea
723: then functions $\Psi_{q\bar q}$ and $\Psi_{qg}$ are given by
724: \bea
725: \Psi_{q\bar q}&=& \frac{2 C_F}{(s^{}_{34} - \mwpsq)^2 +\mwpsq
726: \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2} \left[ R_t \left( -\frac{\ttfp\left( \tot+\stf\right)
727: - \tot\tofp}{\tof} -\frac{\tot\left( \ttfp+\sffp\right) -
728: \ttt\ttfp}{\ttf}\right. \right.  \nonumber \\
729: &&\hspace*{14em}
730: \left. \left. -\frac{\sot\left[ \tot\left( 2\ttfp+\sffp\right) +
731: \stf\ttfp\right] }{\tof\ttf} \right) + R_u
732: \left( p_1 \rightleftharpoons p_2 \right) \right] \nonumber \\
733: &&+ \frac{2 C_F}{(\sot - \mwpsq)^2 +\mwpsq \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2} \left[
734: R_t \left( -\frac{\ttfp\left( \tot+\tof\right) -\tot\ttt}{\stf}
735: -\frac{\tot\left( \ttfp+\ttf\right) \left( 1 - 2 m_t^2/\sffp
736: \right) - \tofp\ttfp}{\sffp}\right. \right. \nonumber \\
737: &&\hspace*{15em}
738: \left. \left. -\frac{\stfp\left[ \tot\left( 2\ttfp+\ttf\right) +
739: \tof\ttfp\right] }{\stf\sffp} \right) + R_u
740: \left( p_1 \rightleftharpoons p_2 \right) \right] \;, \label{eq:psiqq} \\
741: \Psi_{qg}&=& \frac{1}{(s^{}_{34} - \mwpsq)^2 +\mwpsq \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2}
742: \left[ R_t \left( \frac{\sffp\left( \tot+\ttt\right) -\tot\tofp}{\sot}
743: +\frac{\tot\left( \sffp+\ttfp\right) - \stf\sffp}{\ttf} \right. \right.
744: \nonumber \\
745: &&\hspace*{14em} \left. \left. +\frac{\tof\left[ \sffp\left( 2\tot
746: +\ttt\right) +\tot\ttfp\right]}{\sot\ttf} \right) \right. \nonumber \\
747: &&\hspace*{12em} + R_u
748: \left( \frac{\stf\left( \tofp+\ttfp\right) -\tot\tofp}{\sot}
749: +\frac{\tofp\left( \stf+\ttt\right) - \stf\sffp}{\ttf} \right.
750: \nonumber \\
751: &&\hspace*{15em} \left. \left. +\frac{\tof\left[ \stf\left( 2\tofp
752: +\ttfp\right) +\tofp\ttt\right]}{\sot\ttf} \right) \right] \;,
753: \label{eq:psiqg}
754: \eea
755: where $s^{\prime}_{ij}= s_{ij}-m_t^2$, $t^{\prime}_{ij}=t_{ij}-m_t^2$,
756: and all other terms may be obtained by crossing.  Final-state QCD
757: corrections are limited to the second term of $\Psi_{q\bar q}$, and
758: thus this term does not appear in corrections to the leptonic final
759: state.  If the final state is massless, then the solution is recovered
760: by setting $m_t=0$, and noting that all primed invariants are equal to
761: their unprimed counterparts.
762: 
763: 
764: 
765: \subsection{Single-top-quark production via $W^\prime_{R,\,L}$}
766: \label{sec:tottop}
767: 
768: In Sec.~\ref{sec:numwid} we saw that \wpr bosons tend to have a large
769: branching fraction into top quarks.  This observation leads us to
770: consider the effect of such a \wpr on the size of the single-top-quark
771: cross section at hadron colliders.  In particular, we show the cross
772: sections are large enough to improve the mass limits on \wpr bosons
773: using data from run I of the Fermilab Tevatron.  The \wpr boson affects
774: the single-top-quark cross section through the three channels shown in
775: Fig.~\ref{fig:feyn}.  We concentrate on the $s$-channel production,
776: because of the enhancement from the \wpr resonance.  We do not present
777: numerical results for the $t$-channel or associated production of a
778: \wpr boson, because the cross sections for these channels are
779: negligible for the masses we consider.
780: 
781: \begin{figure}[tbh]
782: \epsfxsize=3.4in
783: \centerline{\epsfbox{feyn.ps}} 
784: \caption{Representative Feynman diagrams for single-top-quark
785: production involving a \wpr boson: (a) $s$-channel production, (b)
786: $t$-channel production, and (c) $\wprm \!-t$ associated
787: production.\label{fig:feyn}}
788: \end{figure}
789: 
790: In order to make definitive predictions, we stick to the assumption
791: that the \wpr has purely right- or left-handed interactions.  We
792: choose the standard model CKM matrix as in Eq.~(\ref{eq:ckm}), with
793: the understanding that the final results may be scaled using the
794: factorization of couplings in the last section.  As in
795: Sec.~\ref{sec:numwid}, we choose $m_t=175\pm 5$~GeV,
796: $G_F=1.16639\times 10^{-5}$ GeV$^{-2}$, and $m_W=80.4$ GeV.  For
797: leading-order cross sections we use CTEQ5L \cite{Lai:1999wy}
798: leading-order parton distribution functions (PDFs).  We use a two-loop
799: running of $\alpha_s$, and CTEQ5M1 PDFs for NLO cross sections.  We
800: use the LO and NLO widths calculated in Sec.~\ref{sec:numwid} in the
801: LO and NLO cross sections, respectively, so that all terms are
802: calculated at the same order and with the same method.  We set both
803: factorization and renormalization scales equal to $m_{\wprm}$, since
804: most of the cross section will be produced near resonance.
805: 
806: We present the leading- and next-to-leading order cross sections for
807: single-top-quark production, via $W^\prime_{R,\,L}$ bosons of various
808: masses, at run I of the Tevatron (a $p\bar p$ collider with
809: $\sqrt{S}=1.8$~TeV) in Tables~\ref{tab:sigq} and \ref{tab:sigql}.  In
810: Table~\ref{tab:sigq} we perform the calculation under the assumption
811: that $\nu_R$ is too heavy for the \wpr to decay to leptons, and thus
812: use the widths of Table~\ref{tab:widq}.  In Table~\ref{tab:sigql} we
813: assume all decays are allowed, and use the widths of
814: Table~\ref{tab:widql}.  The cross sections for just top-quark or
815: antitop-quark production are one-half of the listed results.  The
816: corresponding single-top-quark cross sections at a run II of the
817: Tevatron (a $p\bar p$ collider with $\sqrt{S}=1.96$~TeV) appear in
818: Tables~\ref{tab:sigqt} and \ref{tab:sigqlt}.
819: 
820: In Tables~\ref{tab:sigq}--\ref{tab:sigqlt} we show the uncertainties
821: in the cross sections due to the variation of the scale between
822: $m_{\wprm}/2$ and $2m_{\wprm}$, the variation of the top-quark mass
823: over $m_t=175 \pm 5$ GeV including the effects of the change in width
824: listed in Tables~\ref{tab:widq} and \ref{tab:widql}, and uncertainties

840: be an additional $\pm 1$--2\% systematic uncertainty.

\documentstyle[prd,aps,epsfig]{revtex}

\newcommand{\wpr}{$W^\prime$~}
\newcommand{\wprm}{W^\prime}
\newcommand{\wprmp}{W^{\prime\,+}}
\newcommand{\mwpsq}{m^2_{W^\prime}}
\newcommand{\mtsq}{m^2_{t}}

\newcommand{\beq}{\begin{equation}}
\newcommand{\eeq}{\end{equation}}
\newcommand{\bea}{\begin{eqnarray}}
\newcommand{\eea}{\end{eqnarray}}

\begin{document}

\preprint{FERMILAB-Pub-02/165-T}

\title{Fully differential $W^\prime$ production and decay at next-to-leading
order in QCD}

\author{Zack Sullivan}
\address{Theoretical Physics Department, Fermi National
Accelerator Laboratory, Batavia, IL, 60510-0500}

\date{July 23, 2002}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We present the fully differential production and decay of a $W^\prime$
boson, with arbitrary vector and axial-vector couplings, to any final
state at next-to-leading order in QCD.  We demonstrate a complete
factorization of couplings at next-to-leading order in both the
partial width of the $W^\prime$ boson, and in the full two-to-two
cross section.  We provide numerical predictions for the contribution
of a $W^\prime$ boson to single-top-quark production, and separate
results based on whether the mass of the right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$
is light enough for the leptonic decay channel to be open.  The
single-top-quark analysis will allow for an improved direct $W^\prime$
mass limit of 525--550~GeV using data from run I of the Fermilab
Tevatron.  We propose a modified tolerance method for estimating
parton distribution function uncertainties in cross sections.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Since the introduction of the standard model, many extensions have
been proposed that involve enhanced gauge symmetries.  One common
feature of these models is the prediction of additional gauge bosons,
generically called \wpr and $Z^\prime$ bosons.  In non-universal and
top-flavor models, the \wpr gauge boson arises from a new SU(2)$_L$
sector that distinguishes between generations of fermions
\cite{Li:nk,Malkawi:1996fs,Muller:1996dj}, and may treat quarks and
leptons differently \cite{Georgi:1989ic,Georgi:1989xz,He:1999vp}.  The
\wpr boson could be the lowest Kaluza-Klein mode of the $W$ boson
\cite{Datta:2000gm}, or a heavy mass eigenstate in non-commuting
extended technicolor \cite{Chivukula:1995gu}.  In a left-right
symmetric model the \wpr and standard-model $W$ bosons are remnants of
a broken ${\mathrm SU(2)}_L \times {\mathrm SU(2)}_R$ symmetry
\cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974hk,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk}.
The resulting left-right mixing may be naturally suppressed by
orbifold breaking of the left-right symmetry \cite{Mimura:2002te}, or
by supersymmetric interactions \cite{Cvetic:1983su}.  While indirect
bounds may be placed on the masses and couplings of these various \wpr
bosons within the context of their explicit theories, it is always
advantageous to search for these new particles directly.  In order to
facilitate a direct experimental search, and to achieve the most
general contact with theory, we calculate the fully differential
next-to-leading order cross section for the production and decay of a
\wpr boson to any final state with arbitrary vector and axial-vector
couplings.

The most general Lorentz invariant Lagrangian describing the coupling
of a \wpr to fermions may be written as
\beq
{\cal L} = \frac{g}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{f}_i\gamma_\mu \bigl(
C^R_{f_if_j} P_R + C^L_{f_if_j} P_L \bigr) W^{\prime} f_j +
\mathrm{H.c.} \,, \label{eq:genlan}
\eeq
where $P_{R,L}=(1\pm \gamma_5)/2$, $g$ is the standard model SU(2)$_L$
coupling, and the $C^{R,L}_{f_if_j}$ are arbitrary couplings that
differ for quarks and leptons.  For a standard model $W$ boson,
$C^R=0$, and $C^L$ is either the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix or
diagonal, for quarks or leptons, respectively.

Most experimental searches have concentrated on \wpr bosons that decay
via a purely left- or right-handed current.  In order to make contact
with these results, we rewrite Eq.~(\ref{eq:genlan}) in the notation
typical of left-right symmetric models as \cite{Langacker:1989xa}
\beq
{\cal L} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{f}_i\gamma_\mu \bigl( g_R
e^{i\omega} \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} P_R + g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j}
P_L\bigr) W^{\prime} f_j + \mathrm{H.c.} \,, \label{eq:lagrangian}
\eeq
where $\zeta$ is a left-right mixing angle, and $\omega$ is a
CP-violating phase that can be absorbed into $V^R$.  In this notation,
$g_{R(L)}$ are the right (left) gauge couplings, and
$V^{R,L}_{f_if_j}$ are generalized Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (GCKM)
matrices.  In models where the $W$ and \wpr mix, the mixing angle
$\zeta$ is usually constrained to be small ($|\zeta|<$ a few $\times
10^{-5}$--$10^{-2}$ \cite{Groom:in}).  Hence, the search for purely
right- or left-handed states appears well motivated.

Many direct searches for \wpr bosons have been performed at hadron
colliders.  Most experimental analyses have considered left- or
right-handed \wpr bosons, with standard-model-like couplings, that
decay into leptonic final states.  Left-handed $W^\prime_L$ bosons, or
right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons in which the decay into a
right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ is kinematically allowed, are
constrained to have masses $m_{\wprm} > 786$~GeV
\cite{Arnison:1983zy,Arnison:ut,Ansari:1987ch,Albajar:1988ka,Abe:1994zg,Abachi:1995yi,Abe:1999gz,Affolder:2001gr}.
If $m_{\nu_R} \agt m_{\wprm}$ the decay to $\nu_R$ is not allowed,
and the right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons are only directly constrained
by peak searches in the dijet data.  Unless the \wpr has greatly
enhanced couplings to light quarks, the dijet data are limited by QCD
backgrounds to providing a mass limit of $420$~GeV
\cite{Alitti:1990kw,Alitti:1993pn,Abe:1997hm}.

The only final state not measured by one of the experiments listed
above involves the decay of a \wpr to a single top quark.  In
Refs.~\cite{Simmons:1996ws,Tait:1997fe} it was pointed out that a
deviation of measured the single-top-quark cross section from the
standard model prediction could be evidence of a new gauge
interaction.  In the context of models with \wpr bosons, we wish to
take this one step further, and propose that the experiments search
for an explicit \wpr mass peak in the $s$-channel single-top-quark
sample.  We examine just how large the cross section into single top
quarks can be at the Fermilab Tevatron and Large Hadron Collider (LHC)
as a function of \wpr mass, and determine how enhanced or suppressed
couplings enter into the measurable cross section after cuts.  We also
determine the next-to-leading order distributions of the final-state
jets to estimate the effect on the reconstruction of the \wpr mass
peak.

A \wpr boson that propagates in the $s$-channel appears very similar
to Drell-Yan production.  We might be tempted to use the
next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) predictions for Drell-Yan
\cite{Hamberg:1990np} (or the updates in
Ref.~\cite{Harlander:2002wh}).  However, these calculations are not
adequate to predict the cross section for \wpr bosons which decay to
quarks.  There are two reasons for this.  The first problem is that
the final state effects are very large.  Not only are there large QCD
corrections to the quark final state, but the top-quark mass has a
large effect on the branching fraction when it is in the final state.
The second reason is that there are initial- and final-state
interference terms that arise at NNLO that are of an unknown size.
(Pure QCD processes also interfere at NNLO, e.g.\ with $u\bar d \to
u\bar d$ via the exchange of two gluons.)  Therefore, we cannot simply
take the NNLO production as calculated and append a Breit-Wigner
propagator that uses leading or next-to-leading order widths.
Instead, we perform the complete calculation at next-to-leading order.

We organize the paper as follows.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:width} we
calculate the partial widths into leptons or quarks, including the
effects of the top-quark mass, for the \wpr boson using arbitrary
vector and axial-vector couplings at next-to-leading order (NLO) in
QCD.  We demonstrate that the couplings factorize, and present some
numerical results for partial widths and branching fractions into a
top-quark final state.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma} we calculate the fully
differential production and decay of a \wpr into any final state at
NLO in QCD.  We present numerical results for the single-top-quark
production cross section via $s$-channel exchange of a \wpr boson.  We
asses all theoretical uncertainties, and propose a modification of the
tolerance method for calculating parton distribution function
uncertainties.  Finally, we present the NLO jet distributions, discuss
the effect of jet definitions on these distributions, and estimate the
limits that may be placed on the \wpr mass using data from run I and
run II of the Fermilab Tevatron.

\section{Next-to-leading order width}
\label{sec:width}

We divide our evaluation of the \wpr width into three terms that
depend on the final decay products:
\beq
\Gamma_{\mathrm tot}(\wprm) = \Gamma (\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)
+\Gamma (\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime) + \Gamma (\wprm\to l\bar\nu) \,.
\label{eq:widfact}
\eeq
We separate the partial widths containing a top quark from those
containing only massless quarks so that we may retain an explicit
top-quark mass dependence in the width.

While the large number of couplings in Eq.~(\ref{eq:lagrangian})
appears daunting, a factorization of the couplings occurs in the
partial widths of Eq.~(\ref{eq:widfact}) that greatly simplifies the
calculation.  The leading order partial widths are
\bea
\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)&=&
\frac{g^2\beta^2}{16\pi m_{\wprm}} |V^\prime_{tq^\prime}|^2 (m^2_{\wprm}
+ m^2_t/2)\,, \label{eq:wlot} \\
\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
|V^\prime_{qq^\prime}|^2 m_{\wprm} \,, \label{eq:wloq} \\
\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to l\bar\nu)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
|V^\prime_{l\nu}|^2 \frac{m_{\wprm}}{3} \,, \label{eq:wlol}
\eea
where $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, and we assume $g^2=8 m^2_W
G_F/\sqrt{2}$, as in the standard model.  Because we have assumed there
is at most one non-zero mass in the final state, the couplings appear
only in the combination
\beq
\bigl| g V^\prime_{f_if_j}\bigr|^2 \equiv 
\bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 + \bigl| g_R
\cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 \,. \label{eq:vprime}
\eeq
Hence, the partial widths of the \wpr boson have the same form as the
standard model $W$ boson, with the effect of new couplings and GCKM
matrix elements absorbed into $V^\prime_{f_if_j}$.

The above factorization of couplings turns out to hold in the
next-to-leading order widths as well.  The calculations of the
next-to-leading order partial widths of the $W$ boson were first
performed for the massless \cite{Albert:ix}, one mass
\cite{Alvarez:1987gi}, and arbitrary mass \cite{Lahanas:1996xx} final
states many years ago.  In order to derive the factorization of
arbitrary couplings above, however, we rederive the partial widths,
but use a newer calculational method whose results are needed in the
calculation of the fully differential cross section in
Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma}.

We evaluate the next-to-leading order partial widths to quarks by
using the phase-space-slicing method with two cutoffs
\cite{Harris:2001sx}.  In this method, phase space is divided into
three regions: soft (S), hard collinear (HC), and hard non-collinear
(H$\overline{\mathrm C}$).  The first two regions are integrated over
two-body phase space in $n=4-2\epsilon$ dimensions, whereas the third
region is integrated over three-body phase space in 4 dimensions with
cuts.

The soft region of phase space is defined in the \wpr rest frame by
a condition on the energy of the emitted gluon
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appsg}
  E_g \leq \delta_s\, \frac{m_{\wprm}}{2} \,,
\end{equation}
where $\delta_s$ is an arbitrary parameter that must cancel in the
final result.  The hard region is the complement, $E_g > \delta_s\,
m_{\wprm}/2$. The gluon can only be collinear with a light quark, and
so the collinear region is defined by comparing the invariant mass
squared of the gluon and light quark to $\delta_c m^2_{\wprm}$, i.e.\
the collinear region is $s_{qg} = 2p_q\cdot p_g < \delta_c
m^2_{\wprm}$, where $p_{q,g}$ are quark and gluon four-momenta.  The
final result must be independent of $\delta_c$.  In practice we retain
terms logarithmic in $\delta_s$ or $\delta_c$, and drop terms that are
linear in the cutoffs.  At the end, we take the couplings numerically
to zero and show the solution contains no residual $\delta_s$ or
$\delta_c$ dependence.

The two-body next-to-leading order correction to the width is given by
\beq
\delta\Gamma_{2} = \frac{\alpha_s (m_{W^\prime})}{2\pi} C_F ( M^2_S + M^2_C
+ M^2_V + \widetilde{M}^2_V ) \Gamma_{\mathrm LO} \,, \label{eq:wid2}
\eeq
where $C_F = 4/3$, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}$ is listed in
Eqs.~(\ref{eq:wlot}, \ref{eq:wloq}).  If there is a top quark in the final
state, the terms are
\bea
M^2_S &=&2\ln^2(\delta_s) - 2\ln (\delta_s) \left[ 1 - \ln \left(
\frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \right] + \frac{\mwpsq + \mtsq}{\mwpsq -
\mtsq} \ln\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) - 2 {\mathrm Li}_2(\beta)
- \frac{1}{2}\ln^2\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \,,
\label{eq:msf} \\
M^2_C &=& \frac{7}{2} - 2\zeta_2 - \ln^2(\delta_s) + 2 {\mathrm Li}_2\!
\left( \frac{\beta \delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - \ln^2 (\beta) +2 \ln
(\delta_s) \ln (\beta) - \ln (\delta_c) \left( 2 \ln (\delta_s) +
\frac{3}{2} - 2 \ln (\beta) \right) \,, \label{eq:mcf} \\
M^2_V &=& -\frac{1}{2}\ln^2\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) -
\frac{5}{2}\ln\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) - \ln (1 - \lambda)
\left[ 2 + \beta + 2 \ln\! \left(
\frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \right] \nonumber \\
&& - 6 - \ln^2 (1 - \lambda) + 2 {\mathrm Li}_2(\lambda) - 2\zeta_2 \,, 
\label{eq:mvf} \\
\widetilde{M}^2_V &=& \frac{\beta (1-\beta)}{2 (3-\beta)}\ln(1 - \lambda) \,,
\eea
where $\zeta_2 = \pi^2/6$, $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, and $\lambda =
1/\beta$.  Note $(1 -\lambda) < 0$, which means $\ln (1 -\lambda) = \ln
|1 -\lambda|$, but $\ln^2 (1 -\lambda) = \ln^2 |1 -\lambda| - \pi^2$.

If both final-state quarks are massless, the formulae simplify to
\bea
M^2_S &=&4\ln^2(\delta_s) \,, \\
M^2_C &=& 7 - 4\zeta_2 - 2 \ln^2(\delta_s) + 4 {\mathrm Li}_2\! \left(
\frac{\delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - \ln (\delta_c) [ 4 \ln (\delta_s)
+ 3 ] \,, \\
M^2_V &=& - 8 + 4 \zeta_2 \,, \\
\widetilde{M}^2_V &=& 0 \,.
\eea
The sum of the terms in the massless case is
\beq
M^2 = 2\ln^2(\delta_s) - \ln
(\delta_c) [ 4 \ln (\delta_s) + 3 ] + 4 {\mathrm Li}_2\! \left(
\frac{\delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - 1 \,. \label{eq:mmsq}
\eeq

\newcommand{\sttp}{s^\prime_{23}}
\newcommand{\sot}{s^{}_{13}}
\newcommand{\sotp}{s^\prime_{12}}

The three-body hard non-collinear real gluon emission term is evaluated
using a Monte Carlo integration in four dimensions, subject to the
cuts listed above.  The integrand is given by
\beq
d(\delta\Gamma_{3}) = \frac{1}{64\pi^3 m_{W^\prime}}
\overline{\Sigma}|M_3|^2 dE_g dE_{q^{\prime}} \; ,
\eeq
with
\beq
\overline{\Sigma}|M_3|^2 = -2\pi\alpha_s g^2 C_F
|V^{\prime}_{tq^\prime}|^2 \Psi_\Gamma \;,
\eeq
and
\bea
\Psi_\Gamma&=& 
2\beta m_{\wprm}^2 (3-\beta)\biggl( \frac{\sotp}{\sot \sttp}
-\frac{m^2_t}{s^{\prime\,2}_{23}} \biggr) \nonumber \\
&&+ (3-\beta) \biggl(
\frac{\sot}{\sttp} + \frac{\sttp}{\sot} \biggr)
+2 (1-\beta) \;, \label{eq:appwid}
\eea
where $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, $\sotp = 2p_1\cdot p_2$, $\sot =
2p_1\cdot p_3$, $\sttp = 2p_2\cdot p_3$, and $p_1$, $p_2$, and $p_3$
are the four-momenta of the light quark, top quark, and gluon,
respectively.  When both quarks are massless $\beta = 1$, and
Eq.~(\ref{eq:appwid}) is very simple.

Once we determine that the factorization of couplings holds for all
terms, the partial widths reduce to the expressions given in
Ref.~\cite{Alvarez:1987gi} with the replacement of CKM matrix elements
by the GCKM matrix elements $|V^\prime|^2$ defined in
Eq.~(\ref{eq:vprime}).  The massless case is simply
\beq
\Gamma_{\mathrm NLO}(\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime) = \biggl( 1 +
\frac{\alpha_s(m_{\wprm})}{\pi} \biggr) \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to
q{\bar q}^\prime) \,.
\eeq
The massive case should reduce to Eq.~(12) of Ref.~\cite{Alvarez:1987gi},
\bea
\Gamma_{\mathrm NLO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime) &=&
\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime) + \frac{g^2}{16\pi}
\frac{\alpha_s(m_{\wprm})}{4\pi} C_F |V^\prime_{tq^\prime}|^2 m_{\wprm}
\nonumber \\
&&\hspace*{8em} \times\{ \beta(1-\beta)(\beta-4) -
\beta^2(9-5\beta)\ln(\beta) - (1-\beta)
(4+6\beta-5\beta^2)\ln(1-\beta) 
\nonumber \\
&&\hspace*{9em} + \beta^2(3-\beta) [3/2 + 4 {\mathrm
Li }_2 (1-\beta) + 2 \ln(\beta)\ln(1-\beta) ] \} \,. \label{eq:alvwid}
\eea


\subsection{Numerical results}
\label{sec:numwid}

In order to be of immediate use to experimental analyses at the
Fermilab Tevatron, we make definite predictions of the \wpr partial
and total widths.  In all numerical results we use $m_t=175\pm 5$ GeV,
$G_F=1.16639\times 10^{-5}$ GeV$^{-2}$, and $m_W=80.4$ GeV.  We use a
two-loop running of $\alpha_s$ as defined in the CTEQ5M1 parton
distribution functions \cite{Lai:1999wy}.  We assume that
$V^\prime_{l\nu}$ is the identity matrix, and for
$V^\prime_{qq^\prime}$ we use the average Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa
(CKM) matrix \cite{Groom:in} with the exception that we assume
$|V^\prime_{tb}|=1$,
\beq
V^\prime_{\mathrm CKM} = \left(
\begin{array}{llc}
0.9751 & 0.2215 & 0.0035 \\
0.2210 & 0.9743 & 0.0410 \\
0.0090 & 0.0400 & 1.0000
\end{array}
\right) \,. \label{eq:ckm}
\eeq

Before we discuss our results, we must show that our final result does
not depend on the cutoffs we choose.  To demonstrate this, we fix the
ratio of $\delta_s/\delta_c = 300$, and plot in Fig.~\ref{fig:wpss}
the NLO correction to the width of a \wpr of mass 500~GeV.  In the
upper half of the figure we see the logarithmic dependence in

In practice there is a tradeoff between numerical accuracy in
canceling the logarithmic divergences of $\delta_s$ and $\delta_c$ in
the Monte Carlo, and the residual power suppressed dependence on these
parameters.  Hence, we always choose values of $\delta_s$ and

desired Monte Carlo statistical error.

It is not surprising that top-quark threshold effects cause a large
uncertainty in the branching fraction for \wpr masses less than 300
GeV.  This also appears in the large increase in branching fraction at
NLO over the LO branching fraction.  With 33\% changes in both the
mass variation and NLO correction, perturbation theory is somewhat
suspect if $m_{\wprm} \sim 200$ GeV.  However, the effect is less than
10\% by 225 GeV, and rapidly vanishes as $m^2_{\wprm} \gg m^2_t$.  The
branching fraction into a top-quark final state is nearly saturated at
$1/3$ ($1/4$) when $m_{\wprm} \sim 500$~GeV for the quark-only
(quark-plus-lepton) model of decays.  Hence, a large fraction of \wpr
events should produce a top-quark in the final state.  In
Sec.~\ref{sec:tottop} we see this effect on the single-top-quark cross
section.



\section{Next-to-leading order cross section}
\label{sec:sigma}

The analytic form of the differential production and decay of a \wpr
at next-to-leading order is very similar to that of $s$-channel
single-top-quark production.  The complete calculation of differential
single-top-quark production using the phase space slicing method
appears in Ref.~\cite{Harris:2002md}.  We generalize the calculation
in that paper to the production of one massive particle through a \wpr
boson (such that single-top-quark production is a special case).  We
follow closely the notation of Ref.~\cite{Harris:2002md}, but retain
arbitrary couplings in the vertices.  We note that the $t$-channel
exchange of a virtual \wpr is suppressed by at least
$1/m^4_{W^\prime}$, and hence do not consider it here.  However, the
analytic expressions and factorizations that follow are valid for this
channel as well.  The analytic formulae for the $t$-channel exchange
may be obtained by simple crossing.

At leading order, the production of a heavy quark (lepton) may be
written schematically as
\begin{equation}
u(p_1)\bar d(p_2) \to \wprmp \to \bar b(p_3) t(p_4) [\bar l(p_3)
\nu(p_4)] \,,
\end{equation}
where $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$, $u\bar d$ represents all possible parton
fluxes, and the heavy particle in the final state ($t$ or $\nu_R$) has
four-momentum $p_4$ and mass $m$.

The leading-order fully differential spin-averaged partonic cross
section can be written as
\begin{equation}
d\sigma_{0} = \frac{1}{2s} \overline{\sum}
\left|{\cal M}_{0}\right|^2 d {\mathrm{PS}}_2 \,,
\end{equation}
where $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is the partonic center-of-momentum energy
squared, and the two body phase space is given by
\begin{equation}
d{\mathrm{PS}}_2 = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2} \frac{d^3 p_3}{2 E_3} \frac{d^3
   p_4}{2 E_4} \delta^{(4)}(q-p_3-p_4)\, .
\end{equation}

The matrix element squared, summed (averaged) over final- (initial-)
state spin and color states, for production of one massive particle is
\begin{equation}
\overline{\sum} \left|{\cal M}_{0}\right|^2 = \frac{2N_c}{3} \frac{R_t
t\bigl( t-m^2\bigr) + R_u u\bigl( u-m^2\bigr)}{\bigl( s-\mwpsq
\bigr)^2 +\mwpsq \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2} \,,
\end{equation}
where $t=(p_1-p_3)^2$, $u=(p_2-p_3)^2$. The number of colors $N_c=3$,
and $m = m_t$, for a final state with a top quark.  For the production
of a massive neutrino $m = m_{\nu_R}$ and $N_c=1$.  If the final state
is massless, simply set $m=0$ and use $N_c=3$ (1) for quarks
(leptons).  The functions $R_t$ and $R_u$ are given by
\bea
R_t&=&\bigl( |V_i|^2+|A_i|^2 \bigr) \bigl( |V_f|^2+|A_f|^2 \bigr) +
4 {\mathrm Re } (V_i{A_i}^{\!\ast}) {\mathrm Re } (V_f\!{A_f}^{\!\ast}) \,,
\label{eq:rt} \\
R_u&=&\bigl( |V_i|^2+|A_i|^2 \bigr) \bigl( |V_f|^2+|A_f|^2 \bigr) -
4 {\mathrm Re } (V_i{A_i}^{\!\ast}) {\mathrm Re } (V_f\!{A_f}^{\!\ast}) \,,

\label{eq:ru}
\eea
where $V_{i,f}$ and $A_{i,f}$ are the vector and axial-vector
couplings for the initial- and final-state vertices, respectively.  In
the notation of Eq.~(\ref{eq:lagrangian}),
\bea
|V|^2+|A|^2 &=& \frac{\bigl| g_R \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2
+\bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2}{4} \,, \\
2 {\mathrm Re } (V\! A^{\ast}) &=& \frac{\bigl| g_R \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j}
\bigr|^2 -\bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2}{4} \,.
\eea
For right- or left-handed \wpr bosons $|V|=|A|$, $R_u = 0$, $R_t$
reduces to $R_t = \bigl( g^4 |V^\prime_i|^2 |V^\prime_f|^2 \bigr) /8$,
and we recover the standard model $s$-channel single-top-quark cross
section published in Refs.~\cite{Harris:2002md,Harris:2000sv},
including the Breit-Wigner term, up to the GCKM couplings.

We calculate the fully differential next-to-leading order cross
section with the same method used in Sec.~\ref{sec:width}.
Again, the phase space is divided into a hard and soft region, where
the soft region is now defined in the partonic center-of-momentum
frame by a condition of the emitted gluon energy:
\begin{equation}
  E_g \leq \delta_s\, \frac{\sqrt{s_{12}}}{2} \,,
\end{equation}
where $s_{ij}=(p_i+p_j)^2$.  The hard region is the complement, $E_g >
\delta_s\, \sqrt{s_{12}}/2$.  A region is collinear if an invariant
in a propagator is less than $\delta_c s_{12}$, i.e.\ the region is
collinear if in a denominator we obtain $s_{ij} = (p_i+p_j)^2 <
\delta_c s_{12}$, or $t_{ij} = (p_i-p_j)^2 < \delta_c s_{12}$.

At next-to-leading order, color conservation forbids the exchange of a
single gluon between the initial and final states.  This is convenient
when organizing the solution, because the leptonic cross section only
has QCD corrections in the initial state.  Hence, we list separately
the initial and final state corrections.

The two-body NLO correction to the partonic cross section contains
\begin{equation}
d\sigma_2 = \frac{\alpha_s}{2\pi} C_F [(M_S^2 + M_C^2 + M_V^2)d\sigma_0
+d\tilde{\sigma}_V] \,, \label{eq:dsig2}
\end{equation}
where $C_F=4/3$, and $d\tilde{\sigma}_V$ is the part of the correction
to the vertex containing the top quark that is not proportional to the
LO cross section.  If the final state does not contain a top quark
then $d\tilde{\sigma}_V=0$; otherwise,
\begin{equation}
d\tilde{\sigma}_V = (R_t + R_u) \frac{t u}{s^2}\frac{m_t^2 \ln(1-
\lambda)}{\bigl( s-\mwpsq\bigr)^2 +\mwpsq \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2} 
d{\mathrm{PS}}_2 \,.
\end{equation}

The initial-state corrections appearing in Eq.~(\ref{eq:dsig2}) are
\bea
M^2_{S i} &=& 4\ln^2(\delta_s) \,, \\
M^2_{C i} &=& [4\ln(\delta_s) + 3] \ln\!\left( \frac{s}{\mu^2_F}\right)
\,, \\
M^2_{V i} &=& -8+4\zeta_2 \,,
\eea
where $\zeta_2 = \pi^2/6$, and $\mu_F$ is the factorization scale.
If there is a top quark in the final state, $M^2_{S f}$, $M^2_{C f}$,
and $M^2_{V f}$ are the same as those listed in
Eqs.~(\ref{eq:msf}--\ref{eq:mvf}), with the replacements $\mwpsq \to s$,
$\beta \to 1-m_t^2/s$, and $\lambda = 1/\beta$.  If both quarks in the
final state are massless, then $M^2_f$ is given by Eq.~(\ref{eq:mmsq}).

The complete two-body cross section is given by
\begin{equation}
\sigma_2 = \sum_{a,b} \int dx_1 dx_2 \{ f_a^{H_1}(x_1,\mu_F)
f_b^{H_2}(x_2,\mu_F) d\sigma_2^{a b} + [ \tilde{f}_a^{H_1}(x_1,\mu_F)
f_b^{H_2}(x_2,\mu_F) + f_a^{H_1}(x_1,\mu_F)
\tilde{f}_b^{H_2}(x_2,\mu_F) ] d\sigma_0^{a b} \} \,,
\end{equation}
where $a$, $b$ sum over all quark-antiquark luminosities, $\mu_F$ is
the factorization scale, $H_{1,2}$ are the initial-state hadrons, and
the $f(x,\mu)$ are NLO parton distribution functions.  The $\tilde{f}$
functions are introduced to compensate for a difference between the
limits of integration used in the phase space slicing calculation of
the initial-state collinear singularities and the modified minimal
subtraction $\overline{\mathrm MS}$ scheme used in the NLO parton
distribution functions.  The $\tilde{f}$ functions are given in
Ref.~\cite{Harris:2001sx}.


\renewcommand{\sot}{s^{}_{12}}
\newcommand{\stfp}{s^{\prime}_{34}}
\newcommand{\stf}{s^{}_{35}}
\newcommand{\sffp}{s^{\prime}_{45}}
\newcommand{\tot}{t^{}_{13}}
\newcommand{\ttt}{t^{}_{23}}
\newcommand{\tofp}{t^{\prime}_{14}}
\newcommand{\ttfp}{t^{\prime}_{24}}
\newcommand{\tof}{t^{}_{15}}
\newcommand{\ttf}{t^{}_{25}}


The three-body hard non-collinear terms are evaluated using a Monte
Carlo integration in four dimensions, subject to the cuts listed
above.  The cross section is given by
\begin{eqnarray}
\sigma_3 &=& - \sum_{a,b} \int dx_1 dx_2 \frac{4\pi\alpha_s}{s}
\int_{\mathrm H\overline{C}} \{ f^{H_1}_{q_a}(x_1,\mu_F)
f^{H_2}_{q_b}(x_2,\mu_F) \Psi_{q\bar q} \nonumber \\
&&\hspace*{12em} + [ f^{H_1}_{q_a}(x_1,\mu_F) f^{H_2}_{g}(x_2,\mu_F) +
f^{H_1}_{g}(x_1,\mu_F) f^{H_2}_{q_b}(x_2,\mu_F) ] \Psi_{qg} \}
d{\mathrm{PS}}_3 \,.
\end{eqnarray}
If we label the momenta in the three-body processes
\bea
\Psi_{q\bar q}: u(p_1) \bar d(p_2) &\to & \bar b(p_3) t(p_4) g(p_5) \,, \\
\Psi_{qg}: u(p_1) g(p_2) &\to & \bar b(p_3) t(p_4) d(p_5) \,,
\eea
then functions $\Psi_{q\bar q}$ and $\Psi_{qg}$ are given by
\bea
\Psi_{q\bar q}&=& \frac{2 C_F}{(s^{}_{34} - \mwpsq)^2 +\mwpsq
\Gamma_{W^\prime}^2} \left[ R_t \left( -\frac{\ttfp\left( \tot+\stf\right)
- \tot\tofp}{\tof} -\frac{\tot\left( \ttfp+\sffp\right) -
\ttt\ttfp}{\ttf}\right. \right.  \nonumber \\
&&\hspace*{14em}
\left. \left. -\frac{\sot\left[ \tot\left( 2\ttfp+\sffp\right) +
\stf\ttfp\right] }{\tof\ttf} \right) + R_u
\left( p_1 \rightleftharpoons p_2 \right) \right] \nonumber \\
&&+ \frac{2 C_F}{(\sot - \mwpsq)^2 +\mwpsq \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2} \left[
R_t \left( -\frac{\ttfp\left( \tot+\tof\right) -\tot\ttt}{\stf}
-\frac{\tot\left( \ttfp+\ttf\right) \left( 1 - 2 m_t^2/\sffp
\right) - \tofp\ttfp}{\sffp}\right. \right. \nonumber \\
&&\hspace*{15em}
\left. \left. -\frac{\stfp\left[ \tot\left( 2\ttfp+\ttf\right) +
\tof\ttfp\right] }{\stf\sffp} \right) + R_u
\left( p_1 \rightleftharpoons p_2 \right) \right] \;, \label{eq:psiqq} \\
\Psi_{qg}&=& \frac{1}{(s^{}_{34} - \mwpsq)^2 +\mwpsq \Gamma_{W^\prime}^2}
\left[ R_t \left( \frac{\sffp\left( \tot+\ttt\right) -\tot\tofp}{\sot}
+\frac{\tot\left( \sffp+\ttfp\right) - \stf\sffp}{\ttf} \right. \right.
\nonumber \\
&&\hspace*{14em} \left. \left. +\frac{\tof\left[ \sffp\left( 2\tot
+\ttt\right) +\tot\ttfp\right]}{\sot\ttf} \right) \right. \nonumber \\
&&\hspace*{12em} + R_u
\left( \frac{\stf\left( \tofp+\ttfp\right) -\tot\tofp}{\sot}
+\frac{\tofp\left( \stf+\ttt\right) - \stf\sffp}{\ttf} \right.
\nonumber \\
&&\hspace*{15em} \left. \left. +\frac{\tof\left[ \stf\left( 2\tofp
+\ttfp\right) +\tofp\ttt\right]}{\sot\ttf} \right) \right] \;,
\label{eq:psiqg}
\eea
where $s^{\prime}_{ij}= s_{ij}-m_t^2$, $t^{\prime}_{ij}=t_{ij}-m_t^2$,
and all other terms may be obtained by crossing.  Final-state QCD
corrections are limited to the second term of $\Psi_{q\bar q}$, and
thus this term does not appear in corrections to the leptonic final
state.  If the final state is massless, then the solution is recovered
by setting $m_t=0$, and noting that all primed invariants are equal to
their unprimed counterparts.



\subsection{Single-top-quark production via $W^\prime_{R,\,L}$}
\label{sec:tottop}

In Sec.~\ref{sec:numwid} we saw that \wpr bosons tend to have a large
branching fraction into top quarks.  This observation leads us to
consider the effect of such a \wpr on the size of the single-top-quark
cross section at hadron colliders.  In particular, we show the cross
sections are large enough to improve the mass limits on \wpr bosons
using data from run I of the Fermilab Tevatron.  The \wpr boson affects
the single-top-quark cross section through the three channels shown in
Fig.~\ref{fig:feyn}.  We concentrate on the $s$-channel production,
because of the enhancement from the \wpr resonance.  We do not present
numerical results for the $t$-channel or associated production of a
\wpr boson, because the cross sections for these channels are
negligible for the masses we consider.

In order to make definitive predictions, we stick to the assumption
that the \wpr has purely right- or left-handed interactions.  We
choose the standard model CKM matrix as in Eq.~(\ref{eq:ckm}), with
the understanding that the final results may be scaled using the
factorization of couplings in the last section.  As in
Sec.~\ref{sec:numwid}, we choose $m_t=175\pm 5$~GeV,
$G_F=1.16639\times 10^{-5}$ GeV$^{-2}$, and $m_W=80.4$ GeV.  For
leading-order cross sections we use CTEQ5L \cite{Lai:1999wy}
leading-order parton distribution functions (PDFs).  We use a two-loop
running of $\alpha_s$, and CTEQ5M1 PDFs for NLO cross sections.  We
use the LO and NLO widths calculated in Sec.~\ref{sec:numwid} in the
LO and NLO cross sections, respectively, so that all terms are
calculated at the same order and with the same method.  We set both
factorization and renormalization scales equal to $m_{\wprm}$, since
most of the cross section will be produced near resonance.

We present the leading- and next-to-leading order cross sections for
single-top-quark production, via $W^\prime_{R,\,L}$ bosons of various
masses, at run I of the Tevatron (a $p\bar p$ collider with

Table~\ref{tab:sigq} we perform the calculation under the assumption

7: Structured schema for a FeynRules ``.fr`` model file.
8: 
9: This is the shared representation produced by Lagrangian extraction and consumed
10: by the ``.fr`` generator (render.py). Design principle: STRUCTURE the regular,
11: error-prone blocks (M$Parameters, M$ClassesDescription, M$GaugeGroups,
12: M$Information, IndexRange) so an LLM never hand-writes their Mathematica syntax,
13: and CARRY the irregular parts (Lagrangian algebra, mixing blocks, NLO
14: bookkeeping) as verbatim Mathematica strings.
15: 
16: All numeric fields are strings so exact FeynRules syntax survives untouched:
17: rationals like ``-1/3``, decimals like ``1500.``, scientific ``2.5*^-3``.
18: """
19: 
20: from __future__ import annotations
21: 
22: import re
23: from enum import Enum
24: from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Tuple, Union

26: from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator
27: 
28: # A verbatim numeric string: "-1/3", "1500.", "2.5*^-3", "Internal", "Automatic".
29: NumberStr = str
30: 
31: _OPEN = {"(": ")", "[": "]", "{": "}"}
32: _CLOSE = {v: k for k, v in _OPEN.items()}
33: 
34: 
35: def unbalanced(text: str) -> Optional[str]:
36:     """Why ``text`` has unbalanced brackets, or None when it is balanced.
37: 
38:     Mathematica strings ("...") and comments ((* ... *), nested) are skipped. An
39:     unbalanced verbatim string renders into a .fr that FeynRules stops reading
40:     with "Unexpected end of file" or "Invalid syntax", long after the schema
41:     said OK.
42:     """
43:     stack: List[Tuple[str, int]] = []
44:     i, n, depth = 0, len(text), 0
45:     while i < n:
46:         c = text[i]
47:         if depth:                                  # inside a comment
48:             if text.startswith("(*", i):
49:                 depth, i = depth + 1, i + 2
50:             elif text.startswith("*)", i):
51:                 depth, i = depth - 1, i + 2
52:             else:
53:                 i += 1
54:             continue
55:         if text.startswith("(*", i):
56:             depth, i = 1, i + 2
57:             continue
58:         if c == '"':                               # string literal
59:             i += 1
60:             while i < n and text[i] != '"':
61:                 i += 2 if text[i] == "\\" else 1
62:             if i >= n:
63:                 return "unterminated string literal"
64:             i += 1
65:             continue
66:         if c in _OPEN:
67:             stack.append((c, i))
68:         elif c in _CLOSE:
69:             if not stack or stack[-1][0] != _CLOSE[c]:
70:                 ctx = text[max(0, i - 30):i + 1]
71:                 return f"unexpected '{c}' at character {i} (...{ctx})"
72:             stack.pop()
73:         i += 1
74:     if depth:
75:         return "unterminated comment"
76:     if stack:
77:         c, j = stack[-1]
78:         ctx = text[j:j + 30]
79:         return f"'{c}' at character {j} is never closed ({ctx}...)"
80:     return None
81:

83: def _require_balanced(text: Optional[str], where: str) -> None:
84:     if text:
85:         why = unbalanced(text)
86:         if why:
87:             raise ValueError(f"{where}: unbalanced brackets: {why}")

90: # Mass and width values FeynRules reads: a number, or Internal. The renderer
91: # also maps "Automatic" to a numeric placeholder. Anything else ("Auto",
92: # "External", a parameter name) aborts LoadModel with "Wrong width assignment"
93: # or "Wrong mass assignment", or leaks an undefined name into the UFO.
94: _MW_WORDS = {"Internal", "Automatic"}
95: _MW_FUNCS = {"Sqrt", "Pi"}
96: 
97: 
98: def check_mass_width_value(v: Optional[str], where: str) -> None:
99:     if v is None:
100:         return
101:     s = str(v).strip()
102:     if s in _MW_WORDS:
103:         return
104:     names = set(re.findall(r"[A-Za-z$][A-Za-z0-9$]*", s)) - _MW_FUNCS
105:     if re.search(r"[0-9.][eE][+-]?[0-9]", s):
106:         raise ValueError(
107:             f"{where}: value {s!r} uses e-notation, which Mathematica reads as a "
108:             "product with a symbol; write it as \"1.*^12\""
109:         )
110:     if names or not re.search(r"[0-9]", s) or unbalanced(s):
111:         raise ValueError(
112:             f"{where}: value {s!r} is not a number, \"Internal\" or \"Automatic\" "
113:             "(FeynRules rejects anything else, e.g. \"Auto\" or \"External\"); "
114:             "use a numeric string such as \"1500.\" or \"2.5*^-3\""
115:         )

236:     hermitian: Optional[bool] = None
237:     orthogonal: Optional[bool] = None
238:     allow_summation: Optional[bool] = None

241:     def is_tensor(self) -> bool:
242:         return bool(self.indices)

244:     @model_validator(mode="after")
245:     def _check(self) -> "Parameter":
246:         _require_balanced(self.value, f"parameter {self.name} value")
247:         if self.is_tensor:
248:             if self.value is not None:
249:                 raise ValueError(
250:                     f"parameter {self.name}: tensor uses value_rules, not scalar value"
251:                 )
252:             if self.order_block is not None:
253:                 raise ValueError(
254:                     f"parameter {self.name}: order_block forbidden on tensors"
255:                 )
256:         exclusive = [f for f in (self.unitary, self.hermitian, self.orthogonal) if f]
257:         if len(exclusive) > 1:
258:             raise ValueError(
259:                 f"parameter {self.name}: at most one of unitary/hermitian/orthogonal"
260:             )
261:         if (self.unitary or self.hermitian) and self.complex is False:
262:             raise ValueError(
263:                 f"parameter {self.name}: unitary/hermitian require complex=True"
264:             )
265:         if self.orthogonal and self.complex is True:
266:             raise ValueError(f"parameter {self.name}: orthogonal must be real")
267:         if self.parameter_type == ParamType.External and self.complex is True:
268:             raise ValueError(
269:                 f"parameter {self.name}: External params must be real "
270:                 "(split into real/imag or make Internal)"
271:             )

302:     class_members: List[str] = []

304:     width: Optional[MassSpec] = None

308:     antiparticle_name: Optional[Union[str, List[str]]] = None
309:     full_name: Optional[Union[str, List[str]]] = None
310:     propagator_label: Optional[Union[str, List[str]]] = None
311:     propagator_type: Optional[PropType] = None
312:     propagator_arrow: Optional[PropArrow] = None
313:     unphysical: bool = False
314:     definitions: List[str] = []  # VERBATIM Mathematica rule strings
315:     ghost: Optional[str] = None  # U[n] only
316:     goldstone: Optional[str] = None  # S[n] only
317:     weyl_components: List[str] = []
318:     majorana_phase: Optional[str] = None
319:     chirality: Optional[str] = None

322:     def class_label(self) -> str:
323:         return f"{self.spin_type.value}[{self.class_index}]"

326:     def _check(self) -> "ParticleClass":
327:         if self.unphysical:
328:             if self.mass or self.pdg:
329:                 raise ValueError(
330:                     f"particle {self.class_name}: unphysical fields omit mass/pdg"
331:                 )
332:             if not self.definitions:
333:                 raise ValueError(
334:                     f"particle {self.class_name}: unphysical fields require definitions"
335:                 )
336:         if len(self.class_members) > 1:
337:             if not self.flavor_index:
338:                 raise ValueError(
339:                     f"particle {self.class_name}: multi-member class needs flavor_index"
340:                 )
341:             n = len(self.class_members)
342:             for lst in (
343:                 self.pdg,
344:                 self.particle_name,
345:                 self.antiparticle_name,
346:                 self.full_name,
347:             ):
348:                 if isinstance(lst, list) and len(lst) != n:
349:                     raise ValueError(
350:                         f"particle {self.class_name}: list length must equal "
351:                         f"member count ({n})"
352:                     )
353:         charged = {k: v for k, v in self.quantum_numbers.items()
354:                    if str(v).strip() not in ("0", "0.", "0/1")}

356:             raise ValueError(
357:                 f"particle {self.class_name}: a self_conjugate=true (real or Majorana) "
358:                 f"field cannot carry a charge (got {charged}). Make the field complex "

360:             )
